title: Idols and Images
lead: "You must not make yourself an idol" (Exodus 20:4). The ban on images of God and on worship of other gods runs from Sinai and the golden calf through the prophets' mockery of idols to Paul's warnings, and it divided churches over icons.

sections.b: The second word forbids making any carved image or likeness to bow down to (Exodus 20:4–6), and the Covenant Code repeats that Israel must not make gods of silver or gold (Exodus 20:23). The golden calf breaks the command at once (Exodus 32). Deuteronomy explains that Israel saw no form at Horeb, only a voice (Deuteronomy 4:12–19). The prophets mock idols as wood and metal that cannot see or save (Isaiah 44:9–20; Jeremiah 10:1–16; Psalm 115:4–8). Paul says idolaters exchanged the glory of God for images (Romans 1:23), and John ends a letter: "Little children, guard yourselves against idols" (1 John 5:21).
sections.refs: Exodus 20:4–6, 23; Exodus 32:1–6; Deuteronomy 4:12–19; Isaiah 44:9–20; Psalm 115:4–8; Romans 1:23; 1 John 5:21

sections.h: Images in Jewish and Christian practice
sections.b: Ancient synagogues such as Dura-Europos had painted walls, so the ban was read as forbidding images made for worship rather than all art. In the church, the Second Council of Nicaea (787) allowed the veneration of icons, distinguishing honor given to the image from worship due to God alone. At the Reformation, Reformed churches removed images and counted the image ban as a separate commandment, while Lutherans kept them. Archaeologists debate how early Israel's worship was imageless.
